title: The Body and its Members
english: They were hastening to their own banquets, which they were performing with great expense in the church, as if they were rebuking those who had no need, because while others were hungering, they themselves were feasting; for envying the fellowship, they deprived others of their own sight.

Concerning 1 Cor 12:1–2, he now speaks of the energies of the Holy Spirit, which he distributes to each according to his merit, such as to one to evangelize, and to another to prophesy, and to another something else. But through the phrase 'you are led toward the idols,' he demonstrates the greatest difference between prophecy and divination. For in the idols, the possessors do not act soberly by the impure spirit, but are carried up by an impure spirit, proceeding by a non-voluntary will; for this is made clear by the words 'you are led' and 'you are being brought along.' He says, therefore: you know the energy of the impure spirit from which you suffer, but the energy of the Holy Spirit possesses the pure energy. Consequently, the diviner darkens the soul and does not know what he says, but the prophet's soul becomes brighter, and having learned what he did not know, he speaks the things revealed to him. The demon, as an enemy, darkens the soul, but the Spirit, as a benefactor, enlightens the soul as it approaches, which he leads upward.

Regarding 1 Cor 12:3, for all blasphemies against Christ are worked by the evil one who thunders at the soul. This, therefore, he says, to secure those who claim to be God-bearing and who speak against Christ. Since even the legion and the Pythia were naming the Lord Jesus, we do not say that he who says this speaks perfectly—for there are many lords called righteous—but rather [he lacks] the confession of the lordship and sovereignty of Christ over all. Perhaps they said this while being tested, as the devil had brought him to the mountain. Therefore, he does not receive their testimony as if they were unworthy and being tested.

Regarding 1 Cor 12:8–10, the word of wisdom is to understand the things spoken in wisdom of God in prophets and evangelists and to present them to those hearing; the word of knowledge is the revelation...

The height of those hidden things, which one learns in the first place from grace without even knowing, and he says: faith is merely to believe the proclamation; for it is not simply hearing this that constitutes faith, but to receive the things spoken with faithfulness. Discernment of spirits exists because divination has imitated prophecy in that the Holy Spirit seems to foretell in the same way, and He has granted the discernment of these things so as not to be led astray.

Regarding 1 Cor 12:12, he depicts Christ as being composed of many members from the whole body, thereby showing the church through Christ; for since it has been said that Christ is the head of the church and the church is the body of Christ, and He named the church Christ, He shows the lesser from the greater. Regarding 1 Cor 12:14, he says this so that the more humble ones are not overlooked in the church; for even if someone is lesser by nature, he contributes to the commonality of the church. Regarding 1 Cor 12:27, he did not say members from members, but many members from one member; for the head is a member of the whole body. He did not say from members, but from a member; for the head is one member, who is Christ, the head of the church. Since he mentions members and a body, he begins from the more honorable of the other members after the head, namely the apostles. And 'prophet' he says [refers to] those in the church, not those in the Law. Third, 'teachers'. Do not marvel if a teacher is set before those performing healings and powers; for the signs are so that knowledge may be believed, and knowledge is provided through the teachers. 'Will take hold of'—he says this elsewhere: the one presiding with zeal. 'Governments' refers to the ecclesiastical administrations.

Christ is the head of the church, and by 'member' he says the apostles are second members. He says not those in the Law, but those of the church. Because of this, he shows that they thought highly of the gift of tongues, but also in the other gifts. He shows therefore that the greatest is love; for those indeed are gifts and...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in epistulam i ad Corinthios u05-open

title: Tongues, Love, and Perfect Knowledge
english: Those [gifts] are given to the unworthy for the building up of the church, but the achievement of love belongs to the pious man. Therefore he says: lay hold of the better gifts. And I show you a way that leads you to the enjoyment of the superior gifts, namely the way of love; for the one loving fulfills the law. And the one fulfilling the law is well-pleasing. And the one being well-pleasing receives a spiritual gift.

Because he saw them desiring those who possess the gifts, but not warming the love, he teaches that love is the most supreme good; for those gifts are such that even to the unworthy they were given for the building up of the church, but the achievement of love is the own property of the pious man. So he says the way of love leads us to the enjoyment of the superior [gifts]; for what is higher than the gift of love which fulfills all the law?

And what tongue of angels, with whom there is no chest, no larynx, no tongue, no voice? But rather, as Moses says in Deuteronomy, God set limits of nations according to the number of the angels of God—and clearly He set them when He divided into tongues those attempting to build the tower—because they no longer guarded a common concord but, as if they were made strangers to one another by the changes of language, angels were set, so that each might guard the nation to which he was entrusted, and nothing might be consumed or perish. Because of this, he calls the difference of languages the tongues of angels.

And it must be known that just as David says 'bread of angels' not as something for eating, so also 'tongues of angels' is not for speaking; for this too is as ministering to the decree of God. Human language is that which is trained—for this is acquired, unlike the natural kind—but the language of angels is that which is divided into many by nature. I have become a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.

From here it appears that he calls the alternation and difference of languages the tongues of angels; for the one speaking in other tongues to those who do not know them is like a cymbal producing only a sound, without any meaning being shown. He calls human language rhetorical, grammatical, philosophical, intellectual, compositional, technical, and dialectical. But what tongue is it among angels, with whom there is no chest, no larynx, no voice, nor anything else bodily?

Regarding the tongues, he speaks of the differences of languages which the angels established according to the dispersion at the tower, so that each might guard what was entrusted to a nation. Just as we understand a bread of angels to be that which is provided through the command of the angels—not that the angels were eating, but that the angels were commanded to provide—so also the tongues of angels are the differences of languages which angels established. He spoke of the differences of languages as the clanging of a bronze trumpet and a cymbal; for when someone does not know what is being spoken in another language, the speaker is to him like a meaningless cymbal, and the meaning is not made manifest.

Everything that is unknown is called a mystery, but it is revealed by the power of the Spirit. This is one mystery, as he says elsewhere: 'For I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery,' and again, 'Behold, I say a mystery to us.' After a little while he teaches what love is, where he says: 'Love is patient' and the following. Therefore, to show mercy is one thing and to love is another, yet even to give one's substance to the poor and to give oneself up for martyrdom—if this happens through word alone regarding love, it falls into vanity and empty ambition. Therefore, whether we give because of love for the receiver, or because we are giving on behalf of the God who commanded, and whether we bear witness because of love for the Lord, this we must endure. Love never fails, that is, it never slips into sin. The partial is done away when the whole knowledge is given; for we know but a little of the many things still hidden.

As he says, when I was a child, I had the thoughts of an infant, but having passed into a mature man, I have the mind; no longer merely knowing the father as father, but also what kind of father he is. In the same way, that I know now in part, this I shall learn in the perfect time. And what now is as if in a dim mirror, this I shall know clearly in the time. He did not say 'I will know the mysteries then,' which would follow, but 'I shall be known'; for the one who is known by God and made His own, such a one attains the direct sight of the mysteries. Lest all knowledge being revealed to us, there remains to us the believing that all knowledge shall be revealed to us.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in epistulam i ad Corinthios u05-rem-early

title: The distinction between tongues and prophecy
english: They believe in order to hope, but necessary love is to hope so that we do not fall from hope. Therefore he said: love is greater than this; for through love the law is fulfilled.

For if one does not interpret, but only speaks in a tongue and does not manifest the power, as one not possessing this gift of interpretation, he speaks mysteries indeed—for the Spirit provides tongues—and he utters mysteries through the tongues, but he does not build up the church, not understanding what he says. He who speaks in a tongue builds himself up, knowing that what he did not already utter was intelligible; it was a grace of the Holy Spirit in him and he was building up. Just as one speaking in tongues and interpreting is not less than the prophet. Zeal for the prophecy more than the other gifts, he says. And this he said: for to each according to his administration the gifts were given, and in them was what he wished to zealously seek and receive.

But when some speak in tongues, no listener understands. However, even if the things spoken are indistinct to men, the one speaking in the spirit speaks mysteries—for the Spirit provides mysteries through tongues—the one prophesying benefits those who hear, for he speaks clearly to them. The grace is greater if the one speaking in tongues also receives to interpret; for perhaps he did not obtain both. Just as one speaking in tongues and interpreting is not less than the prophet.

What will I benefit you, he says, if I am not able to speak to you either about what was revealed to me by God, or about what he himself knew and understood, or about what he understood through prophets, or about what he knew to advise or teach you? If I speak about these things and you do not understand, what will I benefit you? Observe, for he says, that even in the pipes and lyre, if the sounds are not distinguished, the piping or the lyre-playing is blended together. Nothing is without sound, clearly, a kind of human. He speaks the various gifts of the Holy Spirit spiritually.

If, he says, I speak in a tongue which I do not know, not even knowing its power, I am convinced that I have an unfruitful mind, not having the power of the things said. Let him pray so that he may obtain a double grace, to speak in tongues and to interpret these.

To be a tongue is an operation of the Holy Spirit, but for the mind it becomes fruitlessness because of the inability to understand or be benefited by what is being said. Therefore, he says, this must be done by me: to make clear what is supplied to me through the Spirit for the building up of those hearing, so that the mind is not fruitless by lacking the power of the words. Because if I give thanks with a tongue but no one can understand or benefit from what is said, the listener does not give the 'Amen'. He calls the 'layman' like a soldier who has not yet been baptized. He speaks of clarity of mind and common language. Strive to be perfect, to understand the Scriptures.

It must be noted that the Jews, being required, where God spoke to them in many tongues, they were disobedient and have nothing to show; but we demonstrate that when the Holy Spirit came and distributed tongues, the disobedient Jews were saying, 'They are drunk on sweet wine.' Thus, tongues are a sign not for the believers but for the unbelievers, and prophecy is not for the unbelievers but for the believers. Thus, tongues build up when the hearer learns that the speaker speaks a tongue he did not know; yet he does not receive the building up of the benefit of spiritual teaching because of the lack of understanding, so that no progress is made. For prophecy is for those coming, but regarding these things, the one who happens to be there is not the unbeliever but the faithful one.

The unbeliever has need of the one not knowing the tongue used, and of the one demonstrating that it is the Spirit of God in him. Thus, the tongue was a wonder, but prophecy is a wonder from its outcome, not in the speaking itself. Unbelief is said in two ways in the Divine Scripture: the true unbelief is that of the Greeks, and the little faith is that of the pious. He calls the Greek 'unbelieving', and the 'layman' the soldier who has not yet been baptized; for then they did not say 'catechumens' or 'unbaptized'. He calls them 'Law-abiding' like the other prophets, because they lived according to the Law. What was said to Isaiah then applied when the Spirit descended upon the apostles, and they spoke in tongues and the Jews mocked. It is clear that tongues benefit when the hearer knows that the speaker speaks a tongue he did not know nor learned from men; nevertheless, the matter does not benefit the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in epistulam i ad Corinthios u05-rem-mid

title: The Necessity of the Resurrection
english: The listener is called an auditor because he does not perceive. Prophecy is given to the faithful, speaking of things to come, to those who do not believe by chance but who are faithful. The sign is given to the unbelieving so that he may believe what he sees, but prophecy is given so that he may confirm what is said and bless the Lord. The Greek is called an unbeliever, and the one being catechized is called a fool; and there are places where even the little-believing is called an unbeliever.

Each one, through which grace he has from God, let him build up the church by this. Having said this, he taught that one speaks by the Holy Spirit when he wishes to speak and is silent just as the prophets, not indeed those restrained by an unclean spirit; for they, even when they do not wish to speak, speak things they do not know. Through these things he shows that the Holy Spirit revealed mysteries to the souls, and that to be enlightened there, it was revealed to men, not like in the divinations where the diviner does not know what he utters. Therefore he gave back that first thing which he was saying, that when you were Gentiles toward the mute idols, as you were being led away.

Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others discern, those having the gift of the discerning of spirits. If to another it is revealed while sitting, let the first be silent, as it is in them sometimes to be silent and sometimes to speak. And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. Do not fear, he says, if you keep silent as if rejecting the Spirit; for he knows that the gifts are to be subject to one another. It is manifest that those having the gifts of the discerning of spirits [should use them], so that the church may receive building up and not trouble from all speaking at once.

I say not something foreign, he says, but what I preached. And not only did I preach, but you did not receive, but what also you received. And you did not receive in vain or without foundation, but in which you are being saved. He says that he is about to say that he made known to you that the Lord Jesus died for us; by what word is this gospel, so that the resurrection may be believed; for Jesus is the firstfruits of the resurrection, having died for us. For if death were not to be abolished, the Savior would not have become man, unless in vain he returned.

You received it, instead of 'except that you believed in vain'; for I say that if you do not hold fast, it is evident that you believed in vain. The word of the gospel is the resurrection from the dead, the beginning of which is Christ. For if God did not intend for death to be taken away, He would not have become human. Therefore, if you do not hold fast to what you heard but have rejected it, it is clear that you believed in vain. The term 'instead of' stands for 'but'.

Regarding 1 Cor 15:3, 'In the first place' means 'before all things'; I delivered this to you. 'In the first place' means 'before all things'. I did not deliver a mere argument of my own, but what I received from the Scriptures. It was confirmed by eyewitnesses, that Christ, having died, rose and called him from heaven. Regarding 1 Cor 15:4, how was He buried, if He did not have flesh, according to the heretics? Regarding 1 Cor 15:6, 'instead of' means 'more than'.

Regarding 1 Cor 15:8, an abortion is that which is cast out in the womb before being formed and receiving the time due to it, which also cannot live. Just as in the womb infants are being formed, so in the Law souls were being pre-formed toward piety, and were born of water and Spirit. But Paul persecuted the church without being formed in the Law toward perfection—for he did persecute—therefore he called himself an abortion, and he brings this forth further: because I persecuted the church of God. Infants cast out before being formed in the womb are called abortions. Since in the Law souls were being pre-formed toward piety and were born of water and Spirit, but Paul, as one not having been formed in the Law, persecuted the church, therefore he rightly names himself an abortion.

Regarding 1 Cor 15:9–10a, 'least among the apostles', since he did not persecute them but, having believed, he persecuted. Being a persecutor, he happened to receive such grace according to the foreknowledge of God, so that he labored more than the others. Regarding 1 Cor 15:10b, 'not in vain did I receive much grace', but I used it for the sake of the preaching, laboring more than all of them. 'Instead of' means 'not in vain did I receive the grace'; for I have labored.

Regarding 1 Cor 15:12–13, it is not possible that Christ rose and the rest do not; but, to speak in agreement, if for nothing Christ died and rose, then through nothing is our resurrection. Regarding 1 Cor 15:14–18, he says, if Christ has not been raised, then in vain.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in epistulam i ad Corinthios u05-rem-close

title: The Nature of Resurrection and Death
english: You have believed that the sins of him who forgives are pardoned, even if he has not been raised. But if Christ is raised, just as he indeed is raised, it is evident that the sins are also pardoned, and the resurrection of the dead shall be.

For this reason, we are to be pitied, because we do not inherit the good things of this life. For if we despise the good things of the present life and voluntarily humble ourselves in poverty, temperance, and other things, hoping for other things, how are we not to be pitied, since we inherit the opposites of those things we hope to inherit? He only added to show that piety is a good of the present life. For in this life we serve with piety, and in that life we enjoy the rewards.

Paul asks what kind of death they say the Savior endured, or what kind of resurrection. If either seems so, it is merely an opinion of Christians; but if death is true, then his resurrection is also true. Let them say what kind of death or what kind of resurrection. Is it death by taking on flesh? Surely the Lord had flesh; and if he had flesh, he also died. And if he died, Christ has become the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep having been raised; therefore our own bodies are also raised.

But what kind of death shall I consider? Is it to die to sins? But he himself says: the ruler of this world comes, and in me he has nothing. Even if he died as a sinner and the death of sin, because he took away the sin of the world, by this word he has not risen until today; for he is always a sinner in taking away the sin of the world. But what kind of resurrection does Paul say of the Lord? Is it a deliverance from the flesh? Surely he had flesh. But a deliverance from sins? The same word will be said as before; and if Christ is the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep, it is a necessity that whatever resurrection we give to ourselves, we must also give to the Savior.

What kind of resurrection, then, do we receive? Is it a deliverance from the flesh? Surely the Lord also had flesh. But a deliverance from sins? Surely the Lord also had flesh from which he was delivered. Thus, from every direction, there is the following of the apostolic utterances and power. If the resurrection is of the soul, and its resurrection is understood as a deliverance of the flesh or of sins, how would those who have fallen asleep in Christ be lost, if they were righteous? For if they are in Christ, they are not sinners; and if it is a deliverance from the flesh, the soul is immortal and would not be lost. Do you see that concerning our flesh he says, that which sleeps in Christ, when we die: 'It is good for the one departing'?

Let those who receive these words say through which man death comes, or what kind of death. Is it through Adam? But the soul sinned, while the body was condemned. Furthermore: just as in Adam all die, and so on. He speaks according to the decision regarding the matter; not all are said to have died, for Enoch and Elijah live, and some are found living upon the [earth].

title: The Order of Resurrection and the Kingdom
english: At the presence of the savior, he spoke regarding the decision and the necessity, since not all died like Enoch and Elijah; some will be found even living at the presence. Regarding Adam, he says 'in Adam' instead of 'through Adam', just as in Christ [he says] 'through Christ'. In Adam we die, clearly according to the body, and in Christ we shall be made alive, clearly according to the body; for if souls lived before Christ, and after Christ these alone live again, what is the excess of the economy?

Regarding the rank, he says righteous and unrighteous; he does not say the ones of Christ privately—he does not say the faithful here—but all, because all are of Christ. At his presence there will be the resurrection of all, when also the end occurs, the being baptized by both death and the devil; for this is the end of the world. Regarding the kingdom, he says not his own, but that which the evil one seized, having cast down Adam and those from him. But this he hands over to the Father; he will not be a stranger to it, for the Son co-reigns with the Father.

To rule is not an indication of a deadline but of an appointment, as if someone says: I must live uprightly until I achieve righteousness. He does not say that having achieved it I shall no longer live in righteousness, but that righteousness must be achieved through upright zeal. In the prophets also, 'until' is not necessarily a deadline but a limit, as in the Old Testament where he says: I am, I am until you grow old. He does not say that old age is the limit of his being, but that even if you grow old, I am—not a relative of yours but always being. Thus also now the 'until' signifies the end. What he says is this: his kingdom will not be interrupted in the middle, nor will the believers be taken away until what he set forth is achieved, and having achieved it, he will reign continuously.

If the bodies, he says, remain dead and do not rise, why are we baptized for these dead as if rising and being judged, receiving forgiveness of sins so as not to be judged? As much as I fought with beasts upon a man, God saved me. The Greeks argue that a seed divided no longer grows. Therefore also a man, having his foot cut off or his body entirely amputated, is no longer raised. They are ignorant that it was not nature producing nature that was set forth, but the power of the one who made it; that is, who gave the seed its growing nature and its generative power? Is it not God? Who is the one making the seed die first, and then rise? Is it not God?
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in epistulam i ad Corinthios u06-rem-early

title: The distinction between nature and choice in resurrection
english: Therefore, having given the seed-power to the grain, He gave the strength of resurrection to our own bodies. This was not so that we received a body similar to the fruits and to men, but so that I might demonstrate the creative power.

It is not as the rising of other flesh; for a pattern has been used. He speaks of celestial bodies, the sun and the moon, and shows the things following. So also is the resurrection of the dead. You see that the first things were a pattern; but now that which is the pattern has been given. Regarding celestial bodies, he speaks of the sun and the moon.

He speaks of a psychic body as that which was killed by the sin of the soul, but a spiritual body as that which is raised by the power of the Spirit. This will no longer live according to the weakness of the soul, which is not sufficient to preserve the constitution of the body, but according to the power of the Spirit, which transfers it into immortality. Moses says this: the one who became a living soul, and the second man into a life-giving spirit. This is what the Gospel says; for that which is born in it is from the Holy Spirit.

From the earth is the man according to nature, but earthly according to choice. But concerning Christ he says from heaven: it does not become incorporeal through similarity or through resurrection. Those concerning Valentinus and Marcion, and those from Photius and Apollinaris, allow this, but the explicit word reproves them all. For I ask: did the one from earth, the earthly one, have a soul or not? They will not deny it. And did the Lord from heaven have a body from earth? Again I ask: why does he say the first man from earth is earthly, but the Lord is from heaven?

After these things: as the earthly is, so are the earthly ones; or is it evident that because the one is from earth by nature, and the earthly [is] by choice? Coming to 'as the earthly is', and accusing those who have not lived well, he no longer remembers the nature nor the one from earth, and he no longer says the Lord is from heaven but celestial; again, the spiritual ones were also from earth. As the earthly is, so are the earthly ones, and as the celestial is, so are the celestial ones. And it is necessary, if anyone were to deny that the Lord from heaven took on flesh, since the celestial ones also took on bodies from heaven, because as the earthly is, so are the earthly ones, and thus what is understood is not established at all.

title: The Nature of Resurrection and Transformation
english: Otherwise it is not so. He spoke of nature, from which both those from this earth and the heavenly ones and those called earthly come; but no longer are both of them earthly. Therefore, it is necessary to pay attention to this: that the Lord from heaven is not called 'the heavenly ones,' and the heavenly ones from earth are not 'the Lord from heaven.' He speaks of an image of the earthly, namely the earthly conduct, and an image of the heavenly, namely the heavenly citizenship, so that instead of having imitated the disobedience of Adam, we might imitate also the obedience of the Son of God, having obeyed.

Many of the heretics draw others toward this regarding the resurrection through much folly. For he did not say that flesh and blood do not rise, but rather that they will not inherit the kingdom of God. He excluded the kingdom of the Son of God, not the grace of the resurrection. Therefore, what he says is this: that flesh, being flesh, does not inherit, and blood, being blood, does not inherit; for as long as flesh is flesh, it is corruptible. But having put on incorruptibility, having laid aside the weakness of the flesh, it becomes something else, that is, incorruptible. He proved what he had said before this, for he calls the kingdom incorruption, but calls the mortality in this age corruption. Thus, the opposite of the opposites does not inherit.

He made it manifest that many are trumpets, for having remembered the last, he understood also the first. And the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. If the dead are incorruptible and they themselves shall be changed, it is manifest. What is the need, if we also shall be changed? Or, at any rate, he said that the incorruptible is common to all, while the 'we shall be changed' alludes now to the change into something better; therefore he also said this concerning the righteous.

Having said this and having shown the body, he hemmed in the heretics who say there is no resurrection of the flesh but of the soul. For these also blaspheme concerning the divine economy, thinking that Christ was taken up not in truth but in a phantom, which is senseless. For if he did not have flesh, what is it that died and was buried and was raised? And if these things were a phantom, then surely we also die in a phantom. The incorruptible is indeed common to those who shall be raised, but the changing alone is the particular property of the saints, which shows the change into something better. As for the 'we', it is superfluous, unless he intends to signify concerning the saints, instead of those righteous around us, just as elsewhere, having said 'we', he signified the saints around him, the living ones. The collection is called a collection for the encouragement of the poor.
